Article Title: The Southern Ocean may be Earth’s safest place to remove carbon from the atmosphere, scientists find
Article Text:
Left/Southern Ocean/Right/Southern Ocean on map/Image: AI Generated

Scientists compared climate benefits and ecological risks across the world's major ocean regions

The Southern Ocean delivered the strongest balance between carbon removal and ecosystem protection

Some regions experienced high ecological costs despite removing carbon efficiently

Southern Ocean: Higher carbon-removal efficiency with lower ecological risk.

Equatorial Pacific and global fertilisation: High carbon-removal efficiency but substantially higher ecological impacts.

Subtropical oceans: Lower carbon-removal efficiency accompanied by moderate ecological risks.





Much of the captured carbon eventually returns to the atmosphere

Carbon removal alone cannot determine whether ocean fertilisation should be used

As the world searches for ways to remove carbon dioxide already accumulating in the atmosphere, ocean iron fertilisation (OIF) has emerged as one of the most debated climate intervention strategies. The idea is deceptively simple: adding tiny amounts of iron to iron-poor parts of the ocean stimulates the growth of phytoplankton, microscopic marine organisms that absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. If some of this organic carbon sinks into the deep ocean, it can remain stored for years or even decades. However, scientists have long questioned whether the climate benefits outweigh the ecological risks. A new Nature study finds that the answer depends largely on where fertilisation takes place. While some ocean regions could remove carbon efficiently with relatively limited ecological disruption, others may experience significant and long-lasting impacts on marine ecosystems.The findings come from the Nature study ‘ Climate Benefit and Ecological Cost Trade-offs for Ocean Iron Fertilisation ’ by Jun Yu, J. Keith Moore, Francois W. Primeau, Anthony F. Michaels, Amy G. Nuno, Kristen M.Krumhardt, Michael N. Levy, Keith Lindsay, Hui Wang, James T. Randerson and Adam C. Martiny.Using a process-rich ocean biogeochemical model incorporating validated representations of marine biodiversity and ocean chemistry, the researchers simulated 60 years of ocean iron fertilisation across ten major ocean biomes. Rather than measuring only how much carbon dioxide could be removed, the study also examined changes in biological productivity, oxygen availability, marine food webs and ecosystem recovery after fertilisation stopped.The results revealed that regions capable of removing similar amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide can experience dramatically different ecological consequences.Among all the regions examined, the Southern Ocean consistently offered the most favourable balance between climate benefits and ecological risk.The researchers found that fertilisation in this region produced highly efficient carbon dioxide removal primarily through downstream carbon export, where carbon captured by phytoplankton is transported and stored beyond the fertilised area. Importantly, the surrounding marine ecosystem remained comparatively resilient, with fewer long-term disruptions observed after fertilisation ceased.In contrast, the equatorial Pacific achieved similarly high carbon-removal efficiency through a different mechanism. Here, phytoplankton blooms consumed large quantities of available macronutrients within the fertilised waters, reducing the nutrients carried to downstream ecosystems. This suppressed biological productivity elsewhere, demonstrating that local interventions can generate consequences far beyond the fertilised region.The study shows that maximising carbon removal does not necessarily minimise environmental impacts. According to the researchers, fertilising the equatorial Pacific reduced the flow of energy to higher trophic levels, leading to declines in macrozooplankton biomass. The simulations also showed an expansion of oxygen-minimum zones (OMZs), areas where dissolved oxygen becomes so scarce that many marine organisms struggle to survive.By comparison, similar ecological disturbances were substantially lower in the Southern Ocean, suggesting that relocating fertilisation efforts to higher latitudes could avoid many of the environmental costs identified in lower-latitude oceans.The researchers therefore grouped potential deployment areas into three broad categories:The study also challenges assumptions about how permanent ocean-based carbon removal may be.Across the 60-year simulations, ocean iron fertilisation produced a net atmospheric carbon dioxide reduction of between 1.1 and 5.3 parts per million (ppm). However, the researchers found that more than half of the captured carbon was re-emitted to the atmosphere within decades after fertilisation stopped.Additional recovery tests further emphasised regional variations. Ecosystems in the Southern Ocean usually restored themselves following the conclusion of iron fertilisation, while those in the equatorial Pacific continued to be disturbed because iron stayed within the regional cycle longer, thus sustaining ecological disturbance.This shows that the success of iron fertilisation in oceans is not simply determined by the amount of carbon sequestered but by how long it stays sequestered.However, it can be concluded from the research that evaluation of ocean iron fertilisation is dependent upon considering the impacts of both climatic and ecological dimensions rather than only taking into account the carbon removal dimension.This is due to the fact that ocean currents have a role of moving nutrients and biological variations over large distances, which means that actions taken at one place would influence the ecosystem thousands of kilometres away from there.Rather than identifying a universal solution, the study demonstrates that the success of ocean iron fertilisation depends on where it is deployed. As Jun Yu, J. Keith Moore and their co-authors conclude in ‘Climate Benefit and Ecological Cost Trade-offs for Ocean Iron Fertilisation,’ the Southern Ocean currently offers the most promising balance between meaningful carbon removal and comparatively limited ecological disruption, although significant scientific, regulatory and ethical challenges remain before any large-scale deployment could be considered.
Article Summary: Scientists compared climate benefits and ecological risks across the world's major ocean regions. Southern Ocean delivered the strongest balance between carbon removal and ecosystem protection. Equatorial Pacific and global fertilisation experienced substantially higher ecological impacts. Study shows that maximising carbon removal does not necessarily minimise environmental impacts.

Article Title: German proverb of the day: "A fence lasts 3 years, a dog lasts 3 fences, a horse lasts 3 dogs, and a man lasts…" - a timeless lesson on life's seasons and the value of time
Article Text:
German proverb of the day (AI-generated image)

German proverb of the day

"A fence lasts 3 years, a dog lasts 3 fences, a horse lasts 3 dogs, and a man lasts 3 horses"

What the proverb actually means

Why this old saying still lands today

Five timeless lessons hidden inside this proverb

How this proverb can guide everyday life right now

Why this message still matters now

Final takeaway from the proverb

Some proverbs make their point in a single line. Others need a moment of thought before the meaning actually lands. This old German saying belongs firmly in the second group. On first hearing, it sounds almost like a strange bit of arithmetic involving fences, dogs, horses and people, nothing more. It never quite explains itself outright, and that is really part of its charm. Underneath the odd wording sits a genuinely thoughtful reflection on time, change, and the simple fact that everything living has its own season, whether that happens to be a wooden fence, a family pet, or a person's own lifetime.This is not meant to be taken as an exact measurement of real lifespans. The numbers are symbolic rather than scientific, in keeping with how traditional proverbs generally work, using a memorable comparison to carry an idea rather than a literal fact.The fence stands for something built by human hands, something that slowly wears down through weather and use before eventually needing to be replaced. A dog outlives several fences during its own life. A horse, in turn, outlives several generations of dogs. And a person watches many horses come and go across the course of an entire lifetime.The proverb is really lining up different lifespans side by side to make one simple point, everything exists for a limited stretch of time.Every object, every animal and every person eventually reaches the end of their own particular journey. Rather than reading as gloomy, the saying just accepts that as one of life's steady, unchanging facts.Centuries have passed since this proverb first appeared, and yet its central message still feels oddly familiar. Daily life has changed almost completely. Very few people now rely on horses to get around, or spend their days mending a wooden farm fence. Even so, the actual experience of watching time move forward has not changed one bit.Children grow into adults before parents quite realise how quickly the years slipped by. Grandparents often say life seems to speed up the older they get. Family homes change hands. Beloved pets eventually become nothing but treasured memories. The seasons keep turning with the same steady rhythm they always have, quietly reminding everyone that change is one of the few genuine constants in life.That is probably why this proverb keeps finding new audiences generation after generation. It does not really depend on any one culture or particular era. Its message is rooted in something every single generation ends up experiencing for themselves, the simple passing of time.Time is life's most valuable possession. Money lost can usually be earned again. Belongings lost can often be replaced. Time simply does not work that way. Once a day has gone, it never comes back. The proverb quietly nudges people to notice that every stage of life is temporary, which makes each ordinary day worth a bit more than it might first seem.Change is part of every life, without exception. Nothing stays exactly the same forever. Homes get renovated. Neighbourhoods shift and grow. Families change shape across generations. Accepting that change is coming, rather than constantly fighting it, tends to make life's transitions considerably easier to live through.Gratitude usually starts with the ordinary moments. Plenty of people assume happiness only comes from big achievements. This proverb hints at something far simpler than that. Everyday conversations, shared meals, family gatherings and quiet routines rarely feel remarkable while they are actually happening, yet they usually turn out to be exactly the memories people treasure most once enough time has passed.Every generation leaves something behind, even quietly. A single life is limited, but people rarely vanish without leaving some kind of mark. Parents pass their values on to children. Teachers genuinely shape the students who pass through their classrooms. Friends leave impressions that outlast the specific moments that created them. Even a small act of kindness tends to keep rippling outward long after the moment itself has ended.A meaningful life is measured by more than its actual length. The proverb never claims that simply living longer is the greatest achievement available. Instead, it quietly redirects attention toward how those years actually get spent. A life built on kindness, honesty, curiosity and strong relationships usually leaves a far deeper legacy than one measured purely by numbers on a calendar.The modern world moves at a pace earlier generations could hardly have imagined. Notifications arrive constantly. Work quietly follows people home long after the working day should have ended. Plenty of people spend so much energy preparing for the future that the present slips right past them almost unnoticed.This old German proverb is really just a quiet nudge to pause. It encourages people to actually have the conversation they keep postponing, to visit ageing parents while that chance genuinely still exists, and to look after friendships before distance or busy schedules slowly wear them thin. Small, ordinary choices, sharing a meal without any distractions, taking a walk with someone you love, finally starting a goal you have delayed for years, tend to become exactly the moments people remember most vividly later on.The saying also nudges people toward a healthier relationship with their own possessions. Houses get bigger. Cars get newer. Technology changes almost every single year. All of that has its place, but it rarely becomes anyone's most treasured memory. Relationships, real experiences and time genuinely spent with other people tend to leave a far deeper mark than any of it.Modern life often celebrates speed, productivity and constant achievement, always another target waiting, always another task still to finish. In the middle of that rush, it becomes remarkably easy to forget that life itself is moving forward at exactly the same pace.The proverb is not arguing against ambition or hard work at all. It is quietly asking whether people remember to actually enjoy the years they are working so hard to improve in the first place. Success genuinely matters. So does who that success actually gets shared with.Old sayings like this one survive because they keep answering questions every generation eventually asks for itself. How should time actually be spent. What genuinely deserves attention. What still matters once the years have already passed. This particular German proverb does not offer complicated answers to any of that. It simply reminds people that life is temporary, which is exactly what makes every ordinary day worth appreciating properly."A fence lasts 3 years, a dog lasts 3 fences, a horse lasts 3 dogs, and a man lasts 3 horses" sounds unusual the first time anyone hears it, but its message is both simple and genuinely lasting. Everything in life has its own season, and every generation eventually hands the world over to the next one.Rather than encouraging worry about time passing, the proverb is really an invitation to actually value it while it is still here. Time spent with family, friendships built up slowly over years, lessons passed on to younger generations, and ordinary moments that seem unremarkable at the time, these are, in the end, what actually give a life its greatest meaning. That quiet reminder is exactly what keeps this centuries-old German proverb relevant today.
Article Summary: German proverb of the day: "A fence lasts 3 years, a dog lasts 3 fences, a horse lasts 3 dogs, and a man lasts 3 horses" Centuries have passed since this proverb first appeared, yet its central message still feels oddly familiar. Every object, every animal and every person eventually reaches the end of their own particular journey.

Article Title: Tiny reef fish flourished beside islands filled with seabirds; where rats removed the birds, the entire underwater food chain took another route
Article Text:
Seabirds, rats and small invertebrates

Invasive rats, which arrived as stowaways on ships hundreds of years ago, have decimated the seabird populations on the islands, eating their eggs, chicks and at times even adult seabirds.

Cryptobenthic fish versus invertebrates

This latest study, published in Ecology, is one of the first to reveal the changes to benthic cryptofauna and the species that prey on them.

A changing food web

The researchers found that mixed carnivorous fish rely more on cryptobenthic fish in seabird environments, and that the productivity of fish-eating predators soars while invertivore productivity stagnates near seabirds.

Ecosystems work with each other no matter how far or disconnected they are. Animals and birds have impacts on each other's lives and deaths. According to a new study, invasive rats on tropical islands are creating winners and losers among tiny underwater animals near the bottom of the food chain that inhabit surrounding coral reefs. Now, scientists are saying the resultant changes can rewire food chains on the reefs.Tiny fish and invertebrates that live at the bottom of the sea on coral reefs are known collectively as 'cryptofauna'. These creatures are often overlooked and little studied, but they play a vital ecological role and represent a cornerstone of energy transfer on coral reefs.Led by researchers at Lancaster University and the University of Texas, a team of marine scientists studying these tiny critters on reefs around remote islands in the Indian Ocean have discovered that their populations are much different around islands infested by invasive rats compared to reefs around islands without rats.Reefs surrounding rat-free islands are dominated by tiny 'cryptobenthic' fish species, such as gobies and triplefins, whose biomass is more than five times greater than that of small invertebrates. But around rat-infested islands, the population of small invertebrates such as coral crabs, porcelain crabs and snapping shrimps is higher. Moreover, the biomass of the cryptobenthic fish and invertebrates is nearly equal.The secret to how rats are able to impact these marine creatures lies in how they are affecting the seabird populations on the islands they have infested. Invasive rats, which arrived as stowaways on ships hundreds of years ago, have decimated the seabird populations on the islands, eating their eggs, chicks and at times even adult seabirds. On the islands without rats, the populations of seabirds are a whopping 760 times greater.Seabirds have a vital role in recirculating nutrients from the open ocean where they feed, to the islands where they roost, breed and nest. Their droppings, known as guano, are rich in nutrients that, when washed off the islands into the sea, act as a natural fertiliser for the surrounding coral reef ecosystem.The study area in the Chagos Archipelago in the remote Indian Ocean provides a living laboratory to compare marine ecosystems around islands with and without rats. Researchers from Lancaster University have conducted years of studies looking into the effects of invasive rats on marine ecosystems, from how changes in nutrient flows affect the growth of corals to the territorial behaviour of fish species.This latest study, published by Ecology, is one of the first to reveal the changes to benthic cryptofauna and the species that prey on them, offering surprising new insights for the study team.“Contrary to our expectations, the low-nutrient conditions that rats create do not negatively affect all reef organisms,” said Laura-Li Jeannot, lead author of the study and PhD researcher at Lancaster University. “Nutrient-loss impacts are not uniform. There are winners and losers.“The discovery of the role of cryptic invertebrates is interesting, as really very little is known about these critters, even less so than for cryptobenthic fishes. How they respond to disturbances or transfer energy through systems was almost entirely undocumented,” she said.The researchers believe that fish have a number of competitive advantages when the seabird nutrient flow remains intact. They have extraordinarily high rates of growth and reproduction. “As a result, they have high nutrient and energy requirements, and those can be matched in nutrient-rich environments. This allows these fish populations to flourish and expand in favourable conditions – such as seabird-fertilised reefs,” said Jeannot. With expanding populations, they colonise habitats that would be otherwise occupied by cryptic invertebrates. “Beyond chasing invertebrates away from their homes, they also outcompete them for food: our results show that cryptobenthic fish, when more abundant, likely drive invertebrates to seek alternate, less preferred resources,” she added.On the flip side, the researchers believe that the main reason invertebrates have relative success near rat-infested islands is due to the loss of competitive pressure from cryptobenthic fishes, which are much less abundant in nutrient-poor reefs. Invertebrates' lower metabolic rates could also be an advantage in lower nutrient environments as they don't require as many nutrients to sustain a certain level of biomass.Given the position of cryptobenthic fish and invertebrates near the bottom of the coral reef food chain, researchers expect big impacts on the rest of the food web. “Cryptofauna are the main prey source on reefs, and will often represent the first step in transferring nutrients from primary producers to larger predatory fishes. Any change that affects them is likely to have cascading effects on their predators,” said Laura-Li Jeannot.While much less is known about the role of cryptic invertebrates in wider reef productivity, cryptobenthic fish have been estimated to contribute up to 60% of total consumed biomass on coral reefs, so they are highly important for nutrient and energy cycling on reefs. The researchers found that mixed carnivorous fish rely more on cryptobenthic fish in seabird environments, and that the productivity of fish-eating predators soars while invertivore productivity stagnates near seabirds.“Cryptobenthic fish are a nutrient-dense, protein-packed, highly digestible resource for predators; on the other hand, much of invertebrates’ mass is represented by a tough outer shell. In nutrient-rich environments, fish are also way more abundant than invertebrates, meaning they likely require less foraging. As a result, they represent a more energetically optimal prey near seabird islands for predators looking for a quick snack,” said Assistant Professor Dr Simon Brandl from the University of Texas and co-principal investigator of the study.“These findings suggest a shift in food chains from fish to invertebrate-mediated pathways near seabird-poor islands. Seabird nutrient flows do not just enhance reef productivity and health; they are also influencing trophic structure. Therefore, invasive species like rats that cut off these nutrients can drive significant changes to the food webs of the reefs,” added Professor Nick Graham of Lancaster University and co-principal investigator of the study.These results point out important conservation implications: safeguarding seabirds and their nutrient subsidies is also a way to protect the integrity of reef food webs.
Article Summary: Invasive rats on tropical islands are creating winners and losers among tiny underwater animals near the bottom of the food chain. Researchers found that mixed carnivorous fish rely more on cryptobenthic fish in seabird environments. The productivity of fish-eating predators soars while invertivore productivity stagnates near seabirds.

Article Title: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill 10; missiles hit Poland too
Article Text:
Shocked residents stand outside the building partially destroyed by Russian strikes in the Ukrainian city of Lviv

A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight killed at least 10 civilians, including children, and injured more than 50 others, officials said Thursday, and Nato scrambled its warplanes after one of the missiles crossed the country's western border into Poland.The blitz expanded Russia's almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities, including the capital of Kyiv where tens of thousands spent the night sheltering in subway stations, as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defences.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that North Korean missiles were used in an attack. "In Radushne, the Russians used a missile from North Korea for the first time in a long time - that is what preliminary data shows," Zelensky said in his nightly video address. "The alliance of Moscow b******s with the mad regime in North Korea - for missiles, for the North Korean contingent here in Europe, on our borders, and for the killing of our Ukrainian children. "Nato said a Russian missile entered Polish airspace during the onslaught and landed in a rural area. It caused no injuries or damage but could deepen tensions between the military alliance and Moscow, as wary European countries fear the 4-year-old war could spill into their territory.Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte called it "yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine".Polish PM Donald Tusk said it was "a very serious incident," but added: "There are absolutely no reasons to believe that Poland was the target."Russia's barrage struck areas of Ukraine where weapons are believed to be stored and manufactured. Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia's oil sector, causing a fuel crisis.Zelensky said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities damaged. The Russian defence ministry said it targeted Ukrainian air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities, including drone factories and storage depots. More than 56,000 people sheltered in Kyiv's subway stations overnight, according to the Facebook post from the metro system.(BY REUTERS)
Article Summary: Nato scrambled its warplanes after one of the missiles crossed the country's western border into Poland. The blitz expanded Russia's almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities, including the capital of Kyiv. Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defences.

Article Title: Russia launches overnight ballistic missile attack on Ukraine, killing 13
Article Text:
Photo credit: Reuters

Ukraine expands strikes on Russia's logistics network

Russia launched a wave of overnight air strikes across Ukraine on Thursday, killing at least 13 people, including one in Kyiv. In the attacks that reached as far as the western city of Lviv, prompted neighbouring Poland to scramble fighter jets to secure its airspace.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned about the ballistic missiles heading towards the capital and urged residents to take shelter. Explosions were then heard in Kyiv, according to a Reuters witness. In the western city of Lviv, local officials said two apartment buildings were damaged and six people were injured.The attacks also inflicted heavy casualties elsewhere in the country. Six people, including two children, were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava regions, while in Zelenskyy's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, six more people lost their lives after what local officials said was a direct strike by a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile.Among those killed in Kryvyi Rih were two girls aged 5 and 12. Eight other people were injured in the strike. Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city's defence council, said the missile was launched from Russia's Voronezh region and hit the home of a large family. Describing it as "a dark night", he warned that the death toll could rise as emergency workers continued clearing the rubble.In the western city of Lviv, near the Polish border, rescue workers searched through the debris after Russian missiles damaged two apartment buildings and injured 15 people, according to local officials.Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Russia was likely preparing a massive attack. Following the strikes, he said Ukraine's ability to protect its people depended on its allies willingness to provide more air defence missiles.The appeal came as Zelenskyy returned from the United States, where he said President Donald Trump had agreed to provide Ukraine with licences for Patriot missile systems."It is important that our partners fully understand what is happening and that the protection of people's lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence ​missiles," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.Poland, a member of the European Union and Nato that shares a border with Ukraine, scrambled fighter jets and activated its air defence network as a precaution following the Russian missile strikes.In a post on X, the Polish armed forces said fighter aircraft and an airborne early warning aircraft had been deployed, while ground-based air defence and radar reconnaissance systems were placed on the highest state of readiness to safeguard the country's airspace. The military said the measures were preventive in nature.Ukraine's long-range drone campaign continued to target Russia's logistics infrastructure, with a warehouse belonging to the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries, catching fire in the western city of Penza.Regional Governor Oleg Melnichenko said one person was injured and around 200 people were evacuated after the attack. The incident came just a day after Wildberries was forced to evacuate another facility in central Russia following a separate Ukrainian drone strike.Following the latest attack, Wildberries said it had rerouted its supply chains to minimise disruptions. The company has increasingly become a target of Ukrainian drone strikes, which have repeatedly hit its warehouse network across Russia.According to the company and local authorities, nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses have been damaged in recent attacks, destroying about 10% of its storage capacity and causing losses for tens of thousands of small businesses that rely on the platform.The repeated disruptions have also affected ordinary Russians, many of whom depend on online retail as a primary source of income, while Ukraine's campaign against energy facilities, refineries and logistics infrastructure continues to strain Russia's economy.The financial impact is also being felt in the banking sector. Russia's largest lender, Sberbank, has warned that it may need to increase loan-loss provisions as the sustained attacks on Wildberries weigh on the finances of online retailers and their suppliers.
Article Summary: Poland scrambled fighter jets and activated its air defence network as a precaution following the Russian missile strikes. Ukraine's long-range drone campaign continued to target Russia's logistics infrastructure. A warehouse belonging to the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries, caught fire in the western city of Penza.

Article Title: Is Pakistan facilitating Chinese missile shipments to Iran? Islamabad responds
Article Text:
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir (AP file photo)

Pakistan has pushed back strongly against reports claiming it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran, as Tehran remains locked in a tense standoff with the Donald Trump-led US administration.The rejection by Munir's military comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington, exposing its two-faced tendency in its foreign policy approach.Pakistan’s military chief has recently found favour with US President Donald Trump , while Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.Reacting to reports that Pakistan was set to facilitate the transit of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defence missile systems to Iran, the Trump's "favourite field marshal"-led army dismissed the claims outright.“All such speculations are baseless and devoid of truth,” Pakistan’s military media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, according to Azerbaijan news, citing Anadolu Agency.“Such speculations are categorically rejected,” the ISPR added.The denial came after Reuters reported on Wednesday that Iran was expected to receive its first shipment of Chinese air defence systems within weeks, as Tehran looks to rebuild its defensive capabilities amid its conflict with the United States.According to Reuters, the initial deliveries were planned to move from Urumqi in western China and pass through Pakistan before reaching Iran, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The sources, however, did not clarify whether the transit would take place by air or through land routes.The reports emerged amid speculation over US weapons stockpiles being stretched due to ongoing global conflicts, though Trump later dismissed such concerns. The episode has once again highlighted Islamabad’s delicate balancing act between Beijing and Washington as tensions continue to rise around Iran.
Article Summary: Pakistan denies reports it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran. Comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington. Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.

Article Title: 15-year old sentenced to 100 years in prison for gang-related murder in US
Article Text:
Madison county district attorney's office

A 15-year-old boy has been sentenced to 100 years in prison in the US state of Indiana after being convicted in a gang-related shooting that killed a woman and injured two others last year.According to ABC News, Jo'Majze Larry, of Anderson, Indiana, was sentenced on Wednesday by Judge David Happe of the Madison County Circuit Court. Prosecutors said Larry was one of four alleged members of the Mickey Cobra Nation (MCN) gang charged in the February 2025 killing of 26-year-old Dayla Swain outside Sonny Ray's nightclub in Anderson, near Indianapolis.Investigators said Swain was not the intended target. She was fatally shot during what prosecutors described as a botched hit targeting a witness in another homicide case. Another woman was shot and wounded, while a third was struck by a vehicle as she fled the gunfire.Larry and his co-defendant, 19 year old Rashawn Samuels, were found guilty by a jury on June 30, the Madison County District Attorney's Office said. Samuels was sentenced on Thursday to 125 years in prison.Following their convictions, both Larry and Samuels admitted to an enhancement charge of participating in a criminal organisation.Judge Happe sentenced Larry to 50 years for Swain's murder and imposed an additional 50 year sentence under the criminal organisation enhancement, taking his total prison term to 100 years.Samuels received 62 and half years for the murder conviction and another 62 and half years for the criminal organisation enhancement, bringing his total sentence to 125 years.In a statement, prosecutors said Indiana law provides enhanced penalties for members of criminal organisations because such groups coordinate criminal activity, recruit others to commit crimes and often carry out offences to further the organisation's objectives or for financial gain.A third defendant, 19-year-old Kyree Craver, was convicted of Swain's murder in a separate trial earlier this year and was sentenced to 90 years in prison on July 9. A fourth defendant is expected to stand trial later this year.Larry and Samuels were also convicted of attempted murder and conspiracy to commit murder, prosecutors said.Because Larry was under the age of 18 at the time of the offence, Indiana law allows him to seek a judicial review of his sentence after serving at least 20 years, without requiring the consent of the prosecuting attorney.Prosecutors said the case stemmed from the 2023 killing of 15-year-old Jullian Craig, who was fatally shot during an attempted armed robbery. Donavan Harris, 20, of Anderson, was convicted of Craig's murder in June.According to prosecutors, Craig's killing prompted Larry, Samuels and other alleged gang members to conspire to kill a witness in that case. The planned attack took place on February 2, 2025, outside Sonny Ray's nightclub in Anderson, but instead resulted in the death of Dayla Swain, who prosecutors said was an unintended. victim.
Article Summary: Jo'Majze Larry, of Anderson, Indiana, was sentenced on Wednesday by Judge David Happe of the Madison County Circuit Court. Prosecutors said Larry was one of four alleged members of the Mickey Cobra Nation (MCN) gang charged in the February 2025 killing of 26-year-old Dayla Swain.

Article Title: Man hikes out of mountains to get help after getting impaled by a trekking pole
Article Text:
David Cifaldi impaled himself on a trekking pole while attempting to climb Montana’s highest summit

BILLINGS: David Cifaldi and his two hiking companions were crossing Montana's ominous Froze-to-Death Plateau and approaching the top of the state's highest peak when their adventure took a bizarre and dangerous turn: Cifaldi slipped and impaled himself on his trekking pole as he fell.The 44-inch steel-tipped pole passed through the flesh beneath Cifaldi's left arm, missing any vital organs, and protruded from his back. After conferring with his friends - and considering the high cost of a helicopter rescue - Cifaldi knew who would save him: himself."I was like, 'We've got to get off this mountain.' And they're both like, 'I don't know about that,'" Cifaldi said of his friends' reaction. "I was confident it was outside my chest wall. It was a flesh wound."The 32-year-old nurse, who works at a hospital in Billings, Montana, did a self-assessment. He was alert. There was little pain or blood. And the pole wasn't moving. The group used a satellite-based communication device, a Garmin inReach, to contact local authorities and inform them of their plan to self-rescue.Then they started hiking out. They carefully descended from the plateau along an unmarked route, navigating through boulders and snowfields before bushwhacking their way to an established trail.After more than six hours in which they travelled about 16 kilometres and descended roughly 1,500 metres, the group reached a trailhead where one of them, Cifaldi's friend Jesse Ross, had parked a vehicle. "The only reason it was possible at all was his confidence," Ross recalled. "Who are we to say anything? He's the medical person. Our job was just to support at that point."Cifaldi had long wanted to climb Granite Peak. At 3,900 metres, Montana's tallest mountain is prone to unpredictable weather, including dangerous lightning storms and bitter cold. Hundreds of people annually try to reach the rocky summit; many come up short. As Cifaldi and his companions started hiking out, the pole awkwardly sticking out of his side, Stillwater County Search and Rescue team commander Ty Williams monitored the group's progress via a dispatcher who took calls from the group."There was no danger to anybody else. He didn't want our help and so we didn't force our help on him," Williams said. By about 3.30pm the hikers were in Ross' vehicle headed to the nearest clinic, Cifaldi said.When they arrived, they were told Cifaldi needed more advanced treatment, in Billings. So they got back in Ross' truck and kept driving to the hospital where he works, St. Vincent Regional Hospital. Doctors removed the pole, bandaged him up and Cifaldi was back at work this week."I think 99 times out of a hundred I would make the same decision," Cifaldi said. "Search and rescue coming to help you is free. The flight's not. That was a factor in me deciding to self-rescue. But the fact that I had two experienced great friends with me and we had the ability to contact search and rescue if something went wrong made that a lot more of an easy decision."
Article Summary: David Cifaldi slipped and impaled himself on his trekking pole as he fell. The 44-inch steel-tipped pole passed through the flesh beneath his left arm, missing any vital organs, and protruded from his back. After conferring with his friends - and considering the high cost of a helicopter rescue - he decided to self- rescue.

Article Title: ‘Monumental step toward lasting peace’: Donald Trump announces 'historic' Gaza deal as Board of Peace agrees on Hamas disarmament
Article Text:
File photo: Inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace, in Washington (Picture credit: Reuters)

Phased disarmament, Israeli withdrawal planned

Credits mediators and his team

What is the Board of Peace?

US President Donald Trump on late Thursday (local time) announced that the newly formed "Board of Peace" had reached what he described as a "historic agreement" for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza, saying the phased deal would eventually lead to the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the establishment of a new Palestinian administration.In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the agreement marked "a monumental step toward lasting peace and security" and represented a major milestone in the implementation of his "20-Point Plan" for Gaza."Today, the Board of Peace reached a historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," Trump wrote.According to Trump, the agreement will be implemented in "carefully structured phases", with the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups taking place first."As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbors," he said.Trump added that the arrangement would pave the way for Gaza to be governed by "a new Palestinian government" that would work closely with the Board of Peace."Under this agreement, Gaza will finally be in the hands of a new Palestinian government that serves its people," he wrote.Trump thanked Egypt, Qatar and Türkiye for their mediation efforts, while also praising his administration's role in securing the agreement."I want to thank the mediators—Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye—for their important efforts, and especially my outstanding team, whose tireless work made this historic breakthrough possible," he said.Referring to the October 7 attack on Israel, Trump asserted that Gaza would no longer pose a security threat."The threat that emerged from Gaza on October 7 will not be allowed to rebuild!" he wrote.Trump also said that significant progress had been made over the past year."One year ago there was a violent raging war, humanitarian crisis and hostages kept in brutal captivity. We have made historic progress and there is still much work to do," he said.The announcement comes months after Trump formally launched the Board of Peace during the World Economic Forum in Davos.Initially proposed as part of his Gaza ceasefire initiative, the body was later expanded into a broader international conflict mediation platform.The Board of Peace is chaired by Trump and includes several senior US officials and international figures on its founding executive board, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, special envoy Steve Witkoff, former UK prime minister Tony Blair and Jared Kushner.Around 35 countries had agreed to participate in the initiative, while several traditional US allies, including France, the United Kingdom and Germany, have expressed reservations over its mandate and its potential impact on existing international institutions.Trump concluded his announcement by calling the agreement an unprecedented breakthrough."Congratulations to all on this amazing development, that everybody said could never be achieved!" he wrote.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump announces "historic agreement" for disarmament of Hamas in Gaza. Deal will lead to withdrawal of Israeli forces and establishment of new Palestinian administration. Board of Peace is chaired by Trump and includes senior US officials and international figures on its founding executive board.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Khaled Hosseini: 'A man who has no conscience, no goodness, does not suffer' and why guilt is the starting point for redemption
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Afghan-American novelist Khaled Hosseini.

A man who has no conscience, no goodness, does not suffer.

Beginning of redemption

Other parallels in literature

The Kite Runner, published in 2003, was one of the greatest works of Afghan-American novelist Khaled Hosseini. It tells the story of Amir and Hassan against the backdrop of an unstable Afghanistan. In the novel, Rahim Khan, the moral guide and father figure to Amir says the quote:By the time this conversation takes place, Amir has returned to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan after decades in the United States. He has finally learned the devastating truth that Hassan, his childhood friend whom he betrayed as a boy, was actually his half-brother. Hassan has also been murdered by the Taliban, leaving behind a young son, Sohrab. Amir is consumed by guilt. His entire adult life has been shaped by the shame of one defining moment: he watched Hassan being assaulted and did nothing to help him. Instead of admitting his cowardice, Amir later framed Hassan for theft, causing Hassan and his father Ali to leave Baba's household. Although Amir outwardly built a successful life in America, inwardly he never escaped the weight of his betrayal.Rahim Khan writes this to give Amir a shift in perspective regarding his guilt.He explains that Amir's long-standing remorse and suffering are actually proof that he is fundamentally a good person. A truly evil or sociopathic man feels no guilt, no remorse, and experiences no inner agony over the harm he causes others. Amir's intense suffering demonstrates that he possesses a functioning conscience and a capacity for goodness, which is what ultimately enables him to seek redemption.Though the quote is very specific and has a context, it has universal applicability. the core idea that guilt and emotional suffering are proof of a person's underlying morality resonates across cultures, philosophy, psychology, and literature.Individuals who lack empathy or a moral compass (often characterized by sociopathy or psychopathy) rarely feel genuine remorse for hurting others. They operate without an internal mechanism of self-judgment, meaning they do not experience moral agony over their misdeeds.For the average person, emotional suffering, remorse, shame, sleeplessness, or self-reproach is a natural psychological response to violating one’s own values. Therefore, the pain of guilt itself is evidence that a person still recognizes the difference between right and wrong.Shakespeare famously explored how guilt "makes cowards of us all." Macbeth’s inability to sleep and his descent into mental torment after murdering King Duncan stem directly from his functioning conscience, a sign that he was not inherently evil to begin with, but ruined by ambition. In Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov attempts to prove he is an "extraordinary man" who can commit murder without remorse. His subsequent feverish, agonizing mental breakdown serves as Dostoevsky’s proof that human conscience cannot be intellectually silenced; his suffering is what ultimately leads to his moral salvation.The quote's ultimate power lies in its comforting, redemptive message: suffering from guilt is not a sentence of permanent condemnation; it is the starting point for redemption.It tells anyone haunted by past mistakes that as long as they feel the sting of remorse, their humanity remains intact. It shifts the perspective on guilt from being a meaningless punishment to being an active compass pointing toward "a way to be good again."
Article Summary: The Kite Runner, published in 2003, was one of the greatest works of Afghan- American novelist Khaled Hosseini. The core idea that guilt and emotional suffering are proof of a person's underlying morality resonates across cultures, philosophy, psychology, and literature.

Article Title: A man impales himself on trekking pole while climbing Montana's highest peak, hikes 10 miles to safety instead of calling a helicopter
Article Text:
A man impales himself on trekking pole while climbing Montana's highest peak, hikes 10 miles to safety instead of calling a helicopter

'We've got to get off this mountain'

Six-hour trek with a pole still lodged in his body

Rescue team monitored the situation

Doctors removed the pole and he returned to work

A hiking trip to Montana's highest mountain turned into a remarkable survival story after a nurse accidentally impaled himself on a trekking pole but still managed to hike nearly 10 miles to safety instead of waiting for a helicopter rescue.According to AP, David Cifaldi, a 32-year-old wound care nurse from Billings, was climbing Granite Peak with two friends when he slipped while crossing the notoriously dangerous Froze-to-Death Plateau. During the fall, the 44-inch steel-tipped trekking pole pierced the flesh beneath his left arm, passed through his body, and protruded from his back.Despite the horrifying injury, the pole missed all vital organs.After checking his condition, Cifaldi remained surprisingly calm."I was like, 'We've got to get off this mountain.' And they're both like, 'I don't know about that,'" Cifaldi recalled. "I'm pretty confident this is outside my chest wall. 'Tis but a flesh wound."Working in wound care at a hospital, Cifaldi relied on his medical training to assess the injury. He found that he was fully alert, bleeding very little, experiencing minimal pain, and that the pole was stable rather than moving around inside the wound.The group used a Garmin inReach satellite communicator to contact local authorities, informing them of both the accident and their decision to hike out on their own unless the situation worsened.The three hikers then carefully descended the mountain using an unmarked route, navigating boulder fields, snow patches and thick vegetation before reaching a proper trail.Over the next six hours, they covered nearly 10 miles (16 kilometres) while descending about 5,000 feet (1,500 metres).Friend Jesse Ross, who accompanied Cifaldi throughout the journey, said the nurse's confidence made all the difference."The only reason it was possible at all was his confidence," Ross said. "Who are we to say anything? He's the medical person. Our job is just to support at that point."Stillwater County Search and Rescue commander Ty Williams said authorities received the first call shortly after the accident on July 20.Dispatchers stayed in contact with the hikers throughout their descent as they monitored the group's progress. Since Cifaldi was alert, communicating clearly and repeatedly declined assistance, rescue officials respected his decision."There was no danger to anybody else. He didn't want our help and so we're not going to essentially violate his rights or go against his wishes by forcing our help on him," Williams said.By around 3:30 p.m., the group had reached the trailhead and began driving to the nearest medical facility.Doctors at a local clinic later referred Cifaldi to St. Vincent Regional Hospital in Billings, where he works.There, surgeons safely removed the trekking pole and treated the wound. Just days later, Cifaldi had already returned to work.Looking back, he said he would likely make the same decision again."I think 99 times out of a hundred I would make the same decision," Cifaldi said.While he acknowledged that helicopter transport costs influenced his thinking, he said the biggest reason he chose to self-rescue was that he trusted both his own medical judgment and the experience of the two friends hiking alongside him."I had two experienced great friends with me and we had the ability to contact search and rescue if something went wrong. That made it a lot more of an easy decision," he said.
Article Summary: David Cifaldi, a 32-year-old wound care nurse from Billings, was climbing Granite Peak with two friends when he slipped while crossing the Froze-to-Death Plateau. During the fall, the 44-inch steel-tipped trekking pole pierced the flesh beneath his left arm, passed through his body, and protruded from his back. The pole missed all vital organs.

Article Title: Arizona Sheriff rejects Kash Patel's claim that FBI was kept out of Nancy Guthrie probe for four days
Article Text:
Kash Patel

Dispute over evidence handling





Investigation remains active





The sheriff leading the investigation into the disappearance of Arizona woman Nancy Guthrie has rejected claims by FBI Director Kash Patel that federal agents were prevented from assisting during the crucial early days of the case, saying the bureau was involved from the first day.Speaking on The Sharpe Exchange podcast, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos disputed Patel's recent remarks that the FBI was kept out of the investigation for four days. Nanos said local investigators contacted the FBI's Violent Crime Task Force as soon as search and rescue teams recognised the seriousness of the case."They were there day one just as my team was," Nanos said. "The concept or the representation that the FBI was held off and boy, we wish we'd have been there early on, that's not just even accurate."He added that he believed Patel had been given incorrect information, saying, "I just think he's misinformed."Patel criticised local authorities during an appearance on The Sean Hannity Show, saying the FBI had offered assistance but was unable to participate during the early stages of the investigation."What we, the FBI, do is say, 'Hey, we're here to help. What do you need?'" Patel said. "And for four days, we were kept out of the investigation."He also questioned the decision to send evidence to a private laboratory in Florida instead of the FBI laboratory in Quantico, Virginia."I had a fixed-wing aircraft on the ground ready to move it immediately through the night," Patel said. "We would have analyzed it within days and maybe gotten better information or more information. Our lab's just better than any other private lab out there."The Pima County Sheriff's Department has previously maintained that investigators began working with the FBI "without delay."Nearly six months after 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie disappeared, Nanos said investigators continue to actively pursue the case."We have a lot of evidence that our scientific labs are working," he said, adding that authorities are also reviewing video footage with assistance from private companies while following up on "literally thousands of tips."Nanos also said investigators would immediately disclose any discovery of a burial site, describing such a development as "critical" to the investigation.He added that he would continue supporting Guthrie's family and said if they believe she is still alive, he would share that hope while the investigation continues.
Article Summary: Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos says FBI was involved from the first day. FBI Director Kash Patel said the FBI was kept out of the investigation for four days. Nanos said he believed Patel had been given incorrect information. He added that investigators continue to actively pursue the case.

Article Title: A married lawyer who helped OpenAI beat Elon Musk was caught kissing a 29-year-old colleague; viral video could cost him a multimillion-dollar job
Article Text:
A married lawyer who helped OpenAI beat Elon Musk was caught kissing a 29-year-old colleague; viral video could reportedly cost him a multimillion-dollar job

Viral video sparks controversy

Job move reportedly falls through

Worked on OpenAI's legal victory

Personal life under spotlight

A viral video showing a married New York lawyer kissing a younger colleague in Central Park has reportedly derailed his planned move to another top law firm, putting a multimillion-dollar career opportunity at risk.According to the Financial Times, Nathaniel Cullerton, 45, a partner at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, has been placed on leave while the firm investigates the incident. The report said Cullerton was due to join rival Manhattan law firm Gibson Dunn as part of a high-profile lateral hiring move, but the offer was reportedly withdrawn after the video spread widely on social media.Cullerton was filmed kissing his 29-year-old colleague, Kelsey Borenzweig, on a bench in Central Park. The clip was recorded by TikTok creator Jay Guapo, who interrupted the pair by saying, "Get a room. There's kids around."The two appeared surprised, quickly looking up and attempting to shield themselves from the camera. The video quickly gained traction online, drawing comparisons from some social media users to last year's widely discussed Coldplay concert "cheating scandal."The clip has since been viewed nearly six million times on TikTok and around four million times on Instagram.The timing of the incident proved particularly damaging. According to the Financial Times, Cullerton was expected to leave Wachtell Lipton this week to join Gibson Dunn, following prominent trial lawyer Bill Savitt, who recently moved firms and reportedly brought several senior litigators with him.However, the report said Gibson Dunn withdrew its offer after the kissing video went viral.Legal industry sources told the New York Post that Cullerton likely earns at least $4 million annually as a partner at Wachtell Lipton. While the firm's average partner compensation reportedly stands at around $12 million a year, industry experts noted that junior partners typically earn less than that figure. They also suggested that Cullerton may have been in line for an even more lucrative package at Gibson Dunn.Cullerton and Borenzweig were both members of the Wachtell Lipton legal team that represented OpenAI in its successful defence against Elon Musk 's $150 billion lawsuit in California earlier this year.Their team was led by Bill Savitt, whose move to Gibson Dunn was one of the most significant legal industry departures in recent months.Cullerton is married to prosecutor Moira Kim Penza, who led the federal prosecution that secured the conviction of NXIVM founder Keith Raniere. Public records indicate the couple share an apartment on Manhattan's Upper East Side.It remains unclear whether Cullerton's leave from Wachtell Lipton is paid or what disciplinary action, if any, the firm may take following its investigation.Neither Wachtell Lipton nor Gibson Dunn responded to media requests for comment. Cullerton and Borenzweig have also not publicly commented on the matter.
Article Summary: Nathaniel Cullerton, 45, a partner at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, has been placed on leave while the firm investigates the incident. Cullerton was filmed kissing his 29-year-old colleague, Kelsey Borenzweig, on a bench in Central Park. The clip was recorded by TikTok creator Jay Guapo, who interrupted the pair by saying, "Get a room. There's kids around."

Article Title: US-Iran conflict spreads as new fronts open
Article Text:
TOI correspondent from Washington

: The US-Iran war has entered its most dangerous phase to date. The conflict is now spilling across multiple middle eastern countries and sucking in new combatants – including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Jordan, Egypt and Iraq – in an escalation that military strategists say is beginning to resemble the chain-reaction dynamics that preceded the outbreak of World War I.What began as direct U.S+Israel-Iran hostility has now expanded into a complex regional war stretching from the Red Sea to the Dead Sea and even as far as the Caspian Sea, with Russia and China on the fringes of the conflict. In the latest escalation, US and Saudi Arabian forces jointly struck Iran-backed militias in Iraq after Tehran's allied groups intensified attacks on American and Gulf targets. Iran responded by launching missiles against US military assets in Jordan – claiming to have knocked out three American F-35s – while attacks were also reported in Kuwait and Egypt, underscoring the widening scope of the conflict.The entry of Saudi Arabia into direct military action against Iranian proxies and China’s supply of missiles to Iran mark a significant change in the dynamics of the war. Riyadh had long sought to avoid being drawn openly into a US-Iran war despite years of proxy confrontations. The joint US-Saudi strikes could fundamentally alter the regional balance by making Gulf monarchies active combatants rather than indirect participants.China too reportedly plans to send Iran hundreds of missiles despite U.S warning, with MAGA outlets in U.S fuming that President Xi has “flouted” his promise to Trump. Tehran has claimed that China and Russia have stepped up military assistance, supplying weapons, air-defence systems and other equipment, although the extent of such assistance remains independently unverified. Iranian state media has likewise claimed its forces destroyed several American F-35 stealth fighters operating from Jordanian bases, with no comment, reaction, or denial from Washington so far.Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has widened the maritime battlefield, threatening shipping routes in the Red Sea, from where two tankers with oil for India slipped out this week after going “dark,” highlighting the expanding risk to energy supplies. Commercial shipping and energy infrastructure remain increasingly vulnerable as insurers raise premiums and global markets watch nervously for disruptions to oil exports.Diplomatically, the picture is equally complex. President Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington remains engaged in talks with Iran while Tehran denies there are any talks. The assertions have coincided with fresh American air strikes and increasingly combative rhetoric from the White House and claims of Iranian retaliation that Washington is not confirming.In a recent interview with Fox News, Trump employed coarse language that is becoming his go-to while discussing Iran, -- threatening to beat the f-king s**t out of the country -- remarks unlikely to create an atmosphere conducive to negotiations. Adding another layer of complexity are reports that Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Washington on Wednesday carrying an urgent message from Riyadh urging restraint and warning against allowing the conflict to spiral into a full-scale regional war. At the same time, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Washington during his recent visit to sustain military pressure until Iran's strategic capabilities are decisively degraded.The competing pressures highlight the increasingly difficult position facing the Trump administration amid accounts of growing logistical strains. Reports in recent weeks have suggested that the U.S has been expending precision-guided missiles, interceptor systems and long-range munitions at a pace that is testing production capacity, reviving concerns about stockpile depletion – and preparedness for other conflicts – after years of supporting Ukraine, Israel and other security commitments.Those concerns have intensified as U.S forces conduct sustained operations across multiple theatres despite polls showing Americans are unhappy with the war. Tense White House meetings during which the president reportedly lost his temper over the absence of a decisive military or diplomatic breakthrough are not producing any coherence, while critics are mocking the administration for ending up with “a bombing campaign in search of a strategy. ”For historians, the greatest concern lies not merely in the intensity of the fighting but in its expanding network of participants. The First World War began with a localized crisis before alliance obligations, miscalculations and retaliatory actions transformed it into a global catastrophe. While today's geopolitical landscape is markedly different, diplomats warn that each additional actor – whether state militaries, proxy militias or outside powers supplying arms – increases the risk of unintended escalation, accidental confrontation, and strategic miscalculation.
Article Summary: conflict is now spilling across multiple middle eastern countries and sucking in new combatants – including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Jordan, Egypt and Iraq. Iran responded by launching missiles against US military assets in Jordan – claiming to have knocked out three American F-35s. China too reportedly plans to send Iran hundreds of missiles despite U.S warning.

Article Title: Random Musing: Is Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' a love letter to 'woke' America?
Article Text:
Note: The following piece contains spoilers for both Homer's and Nolan's 'The Odyssey'.

polytropos

Mumbai: Filmmaker Christopher Nolan, centre, interacts with actors Tom Holland, left, and Matt Damon during the premiere of the film The Odyssey, in Mumbai, Maharashtra.

A few years ago, at a popular literature festival, Yann Martel, the author of Life of Pi, made a rather pertinent point about the importance of The Iliad and The Odyssey in Western culture. He argued that, much like the Mahabharata and the Ramayana formed the edifice of Indic civilisation, Homer’s two epics, along with the Bible, were foundational texts of Western civilisation. Perhaps that explains why Musk—who appears to have anointed himself Elon the Lionheart, defender of Western civilisation against wokeness, coloured people and DEI—has been raging against the film ever since the Trojan horse of fake news claimed that Achilles was being played by trans actor Elliot Page Martel isn’t wrong, though, about the impact of Homer’s works, which have stood the test of space, time and language. And almost everyone who has watched the movie—classicists who teach Homer by day, conservatives who think Achilles looked like Brad Pitt and liberals who are raging about the only trans character being killed off in the first scene—agrees on one thing: this is Nolan’s Odyssey, not Homer’s.Now, if you have not read any of the thousands of versions of Homer’s work that exist, here’s a brief recap of the Nolan version.Hollywood has spent billions trying to get Matt Damon home, so Nolan sticks to a tried-and-tested formula that has worked since Saving Private Ryan.To be doubly safe, he decides to retell the story of the Greek man who came up with the wildest tale ever rather than simply telling his wife that he wanted to hang out with his friends instead of coming home to deal with her and their loser son.The wife is played by Catwoman, who, instead of indulging in cat burglary, has taken up arts and crafts. The son is played by Peter Parker, who hasn’t developed his Spidey senses and keeps getting swatted around by everyone in high school. Batman, on the other hand, after dodging the draft, is rather keen on marrying Catwoman and inheriting Jason Bourne’s empire. The Punisher, whose wife happens to be Black Panther’s ex, is still fuming about his better half leaving him to be with Paris. And finally, the guy who fixed John Wick’s car has grown too old to punch nepo kids who try to take things that don’t belong to them.With apologies to both Homer and Nolan for that recap, it doesn’t begin to answer the question posed in the headline. Betteridge’s Law of Headlines states that any headline ending in a question mark can be answered with a “No”, but the answer here is a little more complicated.If you subscribe to Musk’s school of thought, the movie is yet another Hollywood attempt to subvert Americans using the Trojan horse of wokeism—even after it emerged that, despite all the fake news—most of it spread on the hellhole formerly known as Twitter—Elliot Page wasn’t playing Achilles.For the record, Musk has so far endorsed claims that Nolan would be “deemed racist” if he cast a white woman as the “most beautiful woman in the world”; that he had “desecrated” Homer so he could win awards; and that Musk would produce a “historically accurate” AI version that honoured Homer.The last claim drew a sharp rebuke from Nolan, who dismissed the idea that AI could replace human beings and their creativity, calling it a “technology that has been so successfully adopted by Wall Street and by investors and tech companies” but which “the public has so thoroughly rejected”.The complaint about historical inaccuracy is quite preposterous because it is rather like demanding a historically accurate film about Adam and Eve being cast out of heaven or Isaac Newton being hit on the head with an apple.As film critic Alonso Duralde pointed out on a podcast: “There probably wasn’t actually a Helen of Troy…. And if there were, the ancient world was a lot more mixed than we think from all the Italian sword-and-sandal epics we were given in the ’50s and ’60s. You had people from Africa, Asia and Europe. They had boats, y’all!”Did that mean Helen of Troy was black in the modern sense of the term? Probably not. She isn’t a real figure, but a literary construct shaped over millennia of oral poetry, myth-making and retelling. Also, much to the surprise of a lot of folks complaining about coloured characters, the world of Homer wasn’t organised according to modern racial taxonomy.The epics are set in the eastern Mediterranean, not in East Texas. The Aegean, Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt were connected through trade, migration, warfare and intermarriage for centuries before Homer’s poems were even composed. Ports, not borders, defined the ancient Mediterranean. Life wasn’t a Michael Jackson song. Perhaps Musk’s view of Helen’s ethnicity, like those of other MAGA crybabies, is driven by Troy, which came out in 2004 and had the German actress Diane Kruger play Helen.Race-watchers were rather disappointed with Eurylochus, Odysseus’s right-hand man, being played by British-Indian actor Himesh Patel, though, as one X user pointed out, he looked the most “Greek” of all the men with his helmet on.But there are other aspects of the movie that make it feel more like a tribute to 2024 America—when wokeness and DEI madness were at their peak before Trump’s return—than to Homer’s epic.For starters, Nolan takes a protagonist whom Homer describes as, meaning a man of many turns, a many-sided man or a man of many devices: a warrior, king, storyteller, thief, liar, husband, survivor and adulterer. He is a master of adaptability and cunning, with a hubris that angers even the gods. Homer’s poem is fascinated by Odysseus’s self-preserving cruelty, but Nolan instead turns him into a traumatised veteran who sees everything as a personal failure. In the Homeric epic, Odysseus was delighted with his Trojan horse idea, not tormented by destroying his enemy's city.For this author, the scene that truly showed the departure from Homeric themes was the Cyclops scene. In the book, Odysseus and 12 men enter the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus and, after sampling his cheese, the men want to leave, but the hubristic Odysseus refuses because he wants a “guest-gift”. However, Polyphemus dismisses Zeus’s law and proceeds to eat his guests. Odysseus outwits him with some ethanol blending—some exceptionally strong wine—and, when asked his name, says it is Outis, which translates as “Nobody” or “No one”.As the Cyclops sleeps, Odysseus and his men blind him and, when the neighbours come to investigate the commotion, he tells them that “Nobody” is killing him. The neighbours think no human is harming him, but once Odysseus escapes, he makes his most hubristic mistake by taunting Polyphemus and telling him his real name and the name of his kingdom. This allows Polyphemus to pray properly to his father, Poseidon, the god of the sea, who unleashes the hell that follows Odysseus and his men.Nolan said he couldn’t make the “Nobody” pun work, but removing it also removed the most pivotal moment from the epic, completely changing Odysseus from a man who is polytropos into a one-dimensional, morally inflexible and guilt-plagued character with the degree of freedom of a microbe. To put that in context for Indian readers, that’s like taking the character of Karna and removing the Parashurama curse, or removing Yudhishthira’s Ashwatthama hata iti moment.There are other minor modern-day Americanisations. None of the pagan gods causes any havoc, apart from a subdued Athena who appears from time to time. Calypso goes from captor to therapist. Circe the Sorceress, instead of becoming Odysseus’s lover and adviser, becomes a moral judge of his soldiers’ character. But perhaps the most politically coded aspect of the entire plot is the fear of the Sea People. Throughout the movie, people have an abiding fear of unknown invaders called the Sea People who come and rage, a leitmotif that is non-existent in Homer’s work but appears to criticise the conservative fear of open borders and unchecked immigration. By the end, Odysseus admits to Penelope that the Greeks are the “Sea People” and that their ransacking of Troy has thrown the world into disarray and fear.But that’s the beauty of storytelling, of which cinema is just the latest iteration. Stories will always mean different things to different people. The same goes for Nolan’s movie.For classicists, it’s a chance to see someone attempt to show the world what they deal with every day, bringing their entire life’s work to the fore. For people fed up with AI slop, it’s a triumph of human talent. For cinema-goers, it’s the culmination of the “We Are Screwed” trilogy with Tenet, Oppenheimer and The Odyssey. For MAGA, it’s another reason to be angry because the world is somehow slightly different from what they perceive in their heads.And for the rest of us, it’s a beautiful reminder that, no matter what happens and no matter how much technology comes in, some tales are forever, whether told by troglodytes around fires or by Christopher Nolan in 70mm IMAX. Stories are what make us human. And no matter what happens or who makes which movies, Homer’s classics will remain the civilisational grammar of the West, which has seen much better days than its current watered-down version.
Article Summary: Hollywood has spent billions trying to get Matt Damon home, so Nolan sticks to a tried-and-tested formula. The wife is played by Catwoman, who, instead of indulging in cat burglary, has taken up arts and crafts. The Punisher, whose wife happens to be Black Panther’s ex, is still fuming about his better half leaving him to be with Paris.

Article Title: Hyderabad techie killed in US road accident days before India trip
Article Text:
Sripathi Deepa

Family's India visit cut short



Investigation underway

An Indian-origin software engineer from Hyderabad was killed in a road accident in the US state of New Jersey just days before she was due to travel to India, according to reports.Sripathi Deepa Reddy, 42, originally from Aakuthotapalli village in Telangana's Rangareddy district, had been living in the United States with her husband, Ramakrishna Reddy, since 2008. The couple, both software professionals, have two daughters.The crash occurred while Deepa was driving her husband to a metro station. According to preliminary information, another vehicle collided with her car, causing fatal injuries. She died at the scene. Local police have taken the other driver into custody and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash.Deepa was scheduled to fly to India within the next two days, making the tragedy even more devastating for her family. Relatives said the visit had already been planned before the accident occurred.Her family home is located in Teachers Colony, Hastinapuram, in Hyderabad.A video circulating on social media, which has not been independently verified, purportedly shows the aftermath of the crash. Filmed from a passing vehicle, it captures police personnel at the scene along with two heavily damaged cars parked on the roadside.Investigation is underway.
Article Summary: Sripathi Deepa Reddy, 42, originally from Aakuthotapalli village in Telangana's Rangareddy district, had been living in the United States with her husband since 2008. Article Title: Months away from graduation, Indian student sent back home by CBP after phone check, claims viral post
Article Text:
Indian student denied entry to US, asked to leave voluntarily (AI image)

Social media post claims an Indian student was denied entry to the US. He was only a few months away from his graduation.

Can an F-1 student be denied entry to the US?

Inability to show they are a genuine student

Invalid documents

Invalid SEVIS record

Working without authorization

Prior immigration violation

Security, criminal or other inadmissibility grounds

A social media post shared on an NRI group claimed that an Indian student who was returning to the US after visiting India had to deal with an unfortunate situation which ended with a ticket back home. The post claimed that the Webster University student was to graduate this December. He went to India, and on his return, he was stopped after clearing the initial immigration check."He was reportedly stopped for additional questioning by officers, who reviewed his phone and asked about his location history and part-time work," the post said."After questioning, he was advised to voluntarily return to India instead of facing formal removal. He was held for about a day before being sent back to India," the post claimed."He was only a few months away from graduation.
