Article Title: California woman Linda Martin was trimming roses barefoot when a rattlesnake bit her; within 45 seconds tingling reached her jaw and tongue, and three failed 911 calls forced her husband to drive her
Article Text:
Image Credit: CBS LA / YouTube

A growing concern

Need for prompt response

A Stevenson Ranch woman was rushed to the hospital after a rattlesnake that jumped out of her garden bit her. Cutting roses was part of her evening ritual, but it turned out to be nearly fatal.On Saturday evening, 25 July, Linda Martin stepped into her garden as the sun dipped low, ready to prune the roses. “My therapy is cutting roses at the end of the day. I went out and was about to trim a few roses and bring them in,” the woman told CBS. But she never made it past the first bush.“I went and lifted the bush, and that’s when I saw the rattler,” Martin said. With a warning rattle, or hiss, the rattlesnake struck her. The pain was sudden and was followed by a burning sensation. By the time she realised what had happened, her body was already responding. Within 30 to 45 seconds, tingling crept into her fingertips. The sensation spread quickly into her jaw, her cheeks and her tongue. Within a minute, she was on the floor of her home, shaking and trying desperately to call for help. She dialled 911, but the signal failed. She tried again. “Dialled a second time, it didn’t even connect,” she said.Her third attempt finally made it through, but the precious seconds had already slipped away. So her husband asked her to get in the car. He grabbed her and made for Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital. In less than 10 minutes, they arrived at the emergency room, and she was given antivenom. Had he not been home, had he been at work or running an errand, the outcome could have been dramatically different.The woman’s encounter isn’t an isolated incident, according to experts. “Last year, we had a little over 400 calls about rattlesnake bites. And so far, in the first six months of 2026, we’ve had 250 calls,” Lee Cantrell, a director at the California Poison Control System, told the broadcaster. Cantrell added that the state is on track to record 20% more rattlesnake bites this year than last. Five to 10 deaths from venomous snakes occur nationwide annually, he said. This year, California has already logged three deaths.“This year, we had a kind of warm early spring, and so that could have fostered rattlesnakes coming out of hibernation earlier,” Cantrell said.According to Cantrell, rattlesnakes do not have good eyesight. So, when they are hungry and feel warmth nearby, they strike. In Martin’s case, the snake would have mistaken her toe for prey.Though Martin is safe and back home now, she is visibly shaken by the experience. “Had my husband not been home, and I was here alone, I don’t know what would have happened,” she said. She also added that the incident has taught her to push for better mobile service in her community. She is considering reinstalling a landline and is definitely investing in boots for gardening. “I was laughing. Next time in the garden, I’m going to wear a hazmat suit, because I’m afraid to go. But I certainly won’t go gardening without wearing boots,” Martin said.If you are bitten by a snake, medical professionals stress one principle: stay calm and move away from the snake while restricting movement. Restricting movement slows the spread of venom through your body. Do not apply a tourniquet or a heat pad to the wound. Those instinctive responses do more harm than good. Instead, get to a hospital as soon as possible and receive antivenom.
Article Summary: Linda Martin was bitten by a rattlesnake that jumped out of her garden. The pain was sudden and was followed by a burning sensation. Within a minute, she was on the floor of her home, shaking and trying desperately to call for help. Her husband grabbed her and made for Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.

Article Title: Dorinda Medley spent years walking across land she thought belonged to someone else; a survey revealed it was part of Blue Stone Manor, and 3.69 acres are now listed for $1.2 million
Article Text:
Dorinda Medley is selling a parcel from her famous Blue Stone Manor estate (Pictures: Getty images and Bravo)

Land she didn't know she owned

Dorinda Medley tours her extravagant Blue Stone Manor (Picture: Screengrab/Bravo)

A home that became TV landmark

Blue Stone Manor has become one of the most recognisable homes on television after appearing on Bravo's The Real Housewives of New York City. Now, for the first time in more than two decades, a part of the famous estate is being offered for sale.Dorinda Medley, who is best known for starring on the reality television show, is selling a 3.69-acre parcel from her property in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, for $1.2 million. The land is separate from the main house and gives a future buyer the chance to build a home on a site that has long been part of the historic estate.According to the listing, the land has its own private entrance and access road. It is surrounded by protected conservation land and offers views stretching across Massachusetts, Connecticut and New York. The property is also close to downtown Great Barrington."When you're on this property, it's unlike anything you've ever experienced," Medley told People's magazine. "I always say, the minute I go through the gates, time just stops. You leave everything behind. It's like you've entered into a whole different world. It's peaceful and calm and restorative, in a way words can't do justice," she added.According to Medley, she never imagined selling part of Blue Stone Manor.The decision came only after she began reviewing her property as part of her estate planning.She had the estate professionally surveyed for the first time since her late husband bought the property in 2005. The results surprised her. She had believed the estate covered around nine acres, but the survey showed that it actually stretched across nearly 20 acres divided into nine separate lots."I thought to myself, 'Why do I need 20 acres?' I'd been happy with nine! Now I found out I owned 19 and a half!" Medley said.She explained that much of the land was far away from the house and was no longer being used. "I don't want to pay all these taxes on this land I'm not even using. It felt wasteful, because the land I own is so far away from the house," she added,Medley also said she often went for long walks through the wooded trails, believing the land belonged to someone else. "I'd been walking on that land thinking I was trespassing on someone else's property the whole time!" she said with a laugh. "I'd say to anyone who was with me, 'We're gonna walk the horse trails, but I don't know who owns it so we gotta be quick.' Turns out, it's me! I own it!"After the survey, Medley hired a law firm to review the property's easements, topography and building restrictions. The estate was then reorganised into three lots. The parcel now being sold lies beyond the main house, while Medley has kept land closer to the mansion.Blue Stone Manor became famous after appearing in The Real Housewives of New York City. Its grand rooms featured in several memorable moments from the show, including Medley's well-known line, "I cooked, I cleaned, I made it nice."The estate later became the setting for an entire season of Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip. It will also appear again when the cast of Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip: Roaring 20th visits the property for a finale gathering.But for Medley, the home's story began long before television crews arrived. As a child, she dreamed of living in the Tudor-style house, which her grandfather and great-grandfather helped build. She often spoke about the property to her late husband, Richard, and even took him to see the neglected estate.In 2005, shortly before their wedding, Richard surprised her by buying the property. "I'll never forget," Medley recalled. "He takes out the deed with my name on it and says, 'I bought you the house!'" She admitted that her first reaction was shock because she knew how much work the property needed.After buying the estate, the couple invested nearly $4 million restoring the 1902 mansion. The work included lifting the house from its foundation, repairing years of damage, insulating the walls and bringing the old summer home back to life.After Richard died in 2011, Medley continued looking after the estate on her own. She said caring for Blue Stone Manor has required constant attention over the years. Although she is selling part of the land, Medley said the move is about making the estate more practical for the future while preserving its history.As the land goes on the market, Medley hopes its next owner will add a new chapter to the story of Blue Stone Manor while respecting the character that has made it so well known. "The thing that's been the most beautiful thing about Blue Stone Manor is how it resonates with people," she said. "It's not a house, it's a lifestyle. I don't think people really believe it's real. When they finally come up, they don't get it until they get there. It's magic."
Article Summary: Dorinda Medley is selling a 3.69-acre parcel from her property in Great Barrington, Massachusetts. The land is separate from the main house and gives a future buyer the chance to build a home on a site that has long been part of the historic estate. Blue Stone Manor became famous after appearing in The Real Housewives of New York City.

Article Title: California divers spent two years clearing kelp-eating urchins and planting young kelp; underwater forests returned to reefs that had been barren for years
Article Text:
Giant kelp forests once thrived off Southern California's coast. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Why did the kelp forests vanish in California?

Two-year underwater restoration efforts

These vital marine ecosystems vanished due to pollution and overgrazing. A restoration project successfully removed over thirty thousand sea urchins from reefs. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons

From bare reefs to kelp forests

Reasons for the sea urchin problem

More than kelp restoration

Extensive underwater forests of giant kelp once stretched off southern California, providing habitat, food, and breeding grounds for hundreds of marine species, according to NOAA . Over time, these forests gave way to barren reefs because of pollution, habitat destruction and rising sea urchin numbers.One of the project's most successful restoration sites was Escondido Beach. According to the Southern California Giant Kelp Restoration Project report (2002–2009), more than 30,000 sea urchins were removed from the restoration reef, reducing their density from an average of 13 individuals per square metre to 1.5 individuals per square metre.Kelp forests are ecosystems built around rapidly growing giant kelp, which plays an important role in supporting biodiversity. In fact, according to the restoration report, the number of giant kelp in Southern California has decreased by almost 80 percent over the last hundred years.Although storms and El Niño events often damage kelp beds, scientists say restoration is harder because of coastal pollution, sediment from development, overfishing of predators that kept sea urchin numbers in check, and the absence of southern sea otters.The Southern California Giant Kelp Restoration Project was established in 2001 by the California Coastkeeper Alliance, together with Waterkeepers in Southern California and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The programme combined scientific monitoring with active restoration carried out by project biologists and volunteers.One of the most successful restoration sites was Escondido Beach. For about two years, divers spent many hours underwater moving more than 30,000 sea urchins from rocky reefs where kelp forests could be anchored. As a result, sea urchin density dropped from an average of 13 individuals per square metre to 1.5 individuals per square metre.The project also used other restoration methods. These methods included transplanting drifting kelp, planting juvenile kelp grown in the lab and at school, and monitoring the sites over several years. The report says natural predators such as southern sea otters, sheephead fish and spiny lobsters once controlled urchin populations.The findings were significant. According to the project report, the restoration areas outgrew the adjacent natural kelp forest quickly, while the control areas remained urchin barrens. After just one year of relocating sea urchins, some restoration areas had become mature, stable kelp beds, showing that the ecosystem can recover when overgrazing is reduced. The project helped restore about 18,500 square meters of giant kelp forest habitat in Southern California.Sea urchins normally graze on kelp, but balanced ecosystems keep urchin populations in check. The report says natural predators such as southern sea otters, adult sheephead fish, and spiny lobsters once controlled urchin populations. However, the disappearance of these predators led to growth in the urchin population, which in turn destroyed kelp forests. The report notes that, without intervention, urchins can destroy a kelp forest.Along with habitat restoration, the project became one of California's largest community marine conservation efforts. According to the report, hundreds of volunteer divers contributed several thousand underwater hours, while project biologists involved more than 14,000 students in learning about kelp ecosystems. Education campaigns reached more than a million people in Southern California with messages about marine ecosystem protection. The report concludes that kelp forest loss can be reversed by removing sea urchins, transplanting juvenile kelp and monitoring the habitat.
Article Summary: Giant kelp forests once thrived off Southern California's coast. These vital marine ecosystems vanished due to pollution and overgrazing. A restoration project successfully removed over thirty thousand sea urchins from reefs. The project helped restore about 18,500 square meters of giant kelp forest habitat in Southern California.

Article Title: In 1939, a wildlife biologist hiked 1,700 miles through Alaska's Denali to learn why sheep were vanishing; he found winter, not wolves, was to blame
Article Text:
Murie investigated this old trapper’s cabin, 1941. Image Credit: DNP&P Museum Collection via National Park Service

Wolves were vilified for several reasons

Wildlife biologist Adolph Murie studied Dall sheep and wolves in Denali National Park. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Intensive fieldwork in one of America’s most untamed environments

The unexpected conclusion

A study that influenced conservation

Legacy of Denali National Park

A lesson that still matters today

When wildlife populations decline, predators are often blamed. That is what happened in Alaska’s Denali National Park, where Dall sheep numbers fell sharply in the 1930s. Many people thought wolves were to blame and demanded predator control measures. However, a field study by wildlife biologist Adolph Murie challenged that assumption and changed how conservationists understood predators.According to the US National Park Service , Adolph Murie spent two years studying wolves’ effects on the Dall sheep population in Mount McKinley National Park. In the summer of 1939, he walked about 1,700 miles to conduct a major study of wolves in North America.In the early 1930s, fewer Dall sheep were seen in the park. The wildlife management policy in America at the time was mostly predator control, and wolves were generally considered a menace to game.According to the National Park Service, officials wanted scientific evidence before removing wolves from the park. In 1939, Murie was given the task of finding out the relationship between wolves and sheep, which resulted in a study that lasted until 1941. Rather than focusing only on wolves, Murie studied the broader ecology and behaviour of both predator and prey.To carry out his work, Murie relied on field observation rather than technology.According to the National Park Service, he walked through mountains and valleys, watched wildlife with binoculars and telescopes, and made nightly notes in field journals.His study also included analysing wolf scat to identify prey, studying animal skulls and bones to assess age and condition, taking photographs, and examining habitats. According to the National Park Service, Murie had travelled almost 1,700 miles on foot during the summer season of 1939.After about two years of field research, Murie reached a conclusion that contradicted popular belief. As stated by the National Park Service, the decline of Dall sheep was not the result of wolf predation. Severe winter weather had killed off many of the sheep. The wolves mainly preyed on weakened, wounded, or injured sheep, making them part of the natural system rather than the cause of the decline. Predators and prey formed a complex ecological system in which weather, food supply, and habitat were all significant.Murie released his results in 1944 in the form of a government bulletin entitled The Wolves of Mount McKinley. According to the National Park Service, the bulletin became an influential ecological study and one of the first comprehensive scientific examinations of interactions between wolves and other species in the park.The results also influenced management decisions. Instead of continuing predator control programmes, conservation efforts increasingly focused on preserving ecosystems with natural predator-prey interactions.Murie’s contributions went beyond his wolf studies. The National Park Service noted that Murie monitored wildlife in the park for decades, published numerous works on Alaska’s mammals and birds, made educational films, and became an outspoken champion of wilderness preservation.He also opposed several development projects planned in the park during the 1950s. He believed that road construction and other major projects could spoil the area's wilderness. This made him an important figure in shaping conservation policy at Denali National Park. The Department of the Interior recognised his work and awarded him the Distinguished Service Award in 1965. The Murie Science and Learning Center in Denali was named after him.Murie’s study remains relevant because it shows the value of basing conservation on scientific evidence. He spent years collecting data in some of the harshest regions of North America. His study showed that wildlife populations can decline for several environmental reasons, not just one. More than eight decades later, the study is still recognised as an early example of ecosystem-based wildlife management.
Article Summary: Wildlife biologist Adolph Murie studied Dall sheep and wolves in Denali National Park. In the summer of 1939, he walked about 1,700 miles to conduct a major study of wolves in North America. After about two years of field research, Murie reached a conclusion that contradicted popular belief. Severe winter weather had killed off many of the sheep.

Article Title: 11 police personnel, 15 militants killed in overnight attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ANI file photo)

Pakistan suffered a major overnight militant attack on a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving 11 police personnel and 15 attackers dead by early Thursday.The attack targeted the Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire, police official Irfan Khan said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in the border region in recent months.The dead included police officer Diyar Khan, who was leading a reinforcement team to the attacked outpost, according to a statement from the provincial police. More than two dozen police personnel were also injured in the fighting.Police said the militants used heavy weapons to storm the post. Reinforcements heading to the scene were ambushed on the way, with an armoured personnel carrier damaged before officers regrouped and engaged the attackers, eventually forcing them back.Pakistan has seen a steady rise in militant violence in recent years, with the TTP blamed for many of the attacks. Although the group is separate from Afghanistan's ruling Taliban. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan government of sheltering TTP militants, a charge that Kabul has consistently denied.
Article Summary: Attack targeted Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)

Article Title: 'Frustration of their failure': Ex-envoy Vidya Bhushan Soni slams Pakistan over PoK unrest
Article Text:
Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (ANI file photo)

NEW DELHI: As unrest intensified in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) during the region's ongoing elections, former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni said the protests reflected growing frustration among people over Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges.His remarks came after Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India".Speaking to news agency ANI, Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs and hoped that would help it secure economic assistance. "I think again there is a frustration creeping in, in Pakistan. Because they thought that they were playing the mediator role and they thought things would be fine and they would be once again back into business in terms of getting some economic aid, etc. That's not happening," he said.Soni said several groups opposed to the Pakistani government, including Baloch groups and people in PoK, were now putting pressure on Islamabad because they believed the country had reached a difficult position. According to him, Pakistan was more focused on projecting itself internationally as a peaceful nation than solving the problems of its own people."They are the ones who feel that we must put the pressure because now Pakistan is pushed to the wall.And so that's why they are coming out on the street; they are showing their frustration, they're showing their anger, they're showing their patience is running thin," he said.He added that Pakistan should first address the concerns of its own citizens instead of trying to play a larger role on the global stage. "You have to do something about the people, their own people, rather than trying to go and solve the world's problem; first you solve your own problem back home," Soni said.Warning that the unrest was unlikely to end anytime soon, Soni alleged that Pakistan could respond by using force against its own people because its priorities remained focused on international issues. "It has consequences; it will not stop because Pakistan's priority still continues to be international, and they will try to come down heavily through the use of force on their own people," he said.Calling the situation in PoK particularly worrying, Soni said many residents felt their grievances were being ignored, which had deepened their frustration. "The worrisome factor right now is POK because they have seen that their case is not being heard; they are totally ignored. So I feel that it's a frustration of their failure," he said.Meanwhile, the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKAAC), through a series of posts on X, raised concerns over the treatment of injured people and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police personnel during the crackdown. "The treatment of the injured and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police officers raise serious concerns that require urgent scrutiny," the group said.The committee also alleged that civilian property had been damaged during the operation, saying, "The destruction of civilian property raises serious concerns about the conduct of the security forces during the ongoing crackdown." It further claimed that surveillance equipment had been deliberately destroyed, adding, "The deliberate destruction of surveillance equipment raises serious concerns about transparency, accountability, and the preservation of evidence. "Calling for international attention, the JKAAC urged the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions and human rights organisations to examine the footage from the clashes and launch an independent probe. "We call on the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions, and international human rights organisations to examine this footage, independently verify the facts, and support an immediate, independent and impartial international investigation into the recent events in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir," the group said.
Article Summary: Former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni says protests reflect Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges. Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs. Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India"

Article Title: Security forces’ crackdown, civil unrest continue in POK, 20 dead
Article Text:
File photo: PoK unrest

The situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir ( POK ) remains volatile amid mass civilian unrest, election-related violence, and heavy crackdowns by Pakistani security forces. According to sources, Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad.The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured.Amnesty International USA said that the disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot were consistent with Pakistani authorities’ “long history of unlawful violence against protesters”. “We urge the Pakistani authorities torestore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area,” it said.While security forces continue to maintain a heightened presence in Rawalakot, Muzaffarabad and other areas, sources said the possibility of additional protests remains high over the coming days because of declining public confidence in the political process.Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
Article Summary: Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad. The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured. Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
